sources.text:
Any operating system is likely to run with more processes than the computer has CPUs, so a plan is needed to time-share the CPUs among the processes. Ideally the sharing would be transparent to user processes. A common approach is to provide each process with the illusion that it has its own virtual CPU by multiplexing the processes onto the hardware CPUs. This chapter explains how xv6 achieves this multiplexing.

8.1 Multiplexing

Xv6 multiplexes by switching each CPU from one process to another in two situations. First, xv6 switches when a process makes a system call that blocks (has to wait), for example read or wait. Second, xv6 periodically forces a switch to cope with processes that compute for long periods without blocking. The former are called voluntary switches, the latter involuntary.

Implementing multiplexing poses a few challenges. First, how to switch from one process to another? The basic idea is to save and restore CPU registers, though the fact that this cannot be expressed in C makes it tricky. Second, how to force switches in a way that is transparent to user processes? Xv6 uses the standard technique in which a hardware timer’s interrupts drive context switches. Third, all of the CPUs switch among the same set of processes, so a locking plan is necessary to avoid mistakes such as two CPUs deciding to run the same process at the same time. Fourth, a process’s memory and other resources must be freed when the process exits, but it cannot finish all of this itself. Fifth, each CPU of a multi-core machine must remember which process it is executing so that system calls affect the correct process’s kernel state.

8.2 Context switch overview

The term “context switch” refers to the steps involved in a CPU leaving off execution of one kernel thread (usually for later resumption), and resuming execution of a different kernel thread; this switching is the heart of multiplexing. Xv6 does not directly context switch from one process’s kernel thread to another process’s kernel thread; instead, a kernel thread gives up the CPU by context-switching to that CPU’s “scheduler thread,” and the scheduler thread picks a different process’s kernel thread to run, and context-switches to that thread.

At a broader scope, the steps involved in switching from one user process to another are illustrated in Figure 8.1: a trap (system call or interrupt) from the old process’s user space to its kernel thread, a context switch to the current CPU’s scheduler thread, a context switch to a new process’s kernel thread, and a trap return to the user-level process.

8.3 Code: Context switching

The function swtch() in kernel/swtch.S contains the heart of thread context switching: it saves the switched-from thread’s CPU registers, and restores the previously-saved registers of the switched-to thread. The basic reason this is sufficient is that a thread’s state consist of data in memory (e.g. its stack) plus its CPU registers; thread memory need not saved and restored because different threads keep their data in different areas of RAM; but the CPU has only one set of registers so they must be switched (saved and restored) between threads.

Each thread’s struct proc includes a struct context that holds the thread’s saved registers when it is not running. A CPU’s scheduler thread’s struct context is in that CPU’s struct cpu. When thread X wishes to switch to thread Y, thread X calls swtch(&X’s context, &Y’s context). swtch() saves the current CPU registers in X’s context, then loads the content of Y’s context into the CPU registers, then returns.

swtch saves callee-saved registers (ra,sp,s0..s11) but not caller-saved registers. The RISC-V calling convention requires that if code needs to preserve the value in a caller-saved register across a function call, the compiler must generate instructions that save the register to the stack before the function call, and restore from the stack when the function returns. So swtch can rely on the function that called it having already saved the caller-saved registers (either that, or the calling function didn’t need the values in the registers).

questions.stem:
Paragraph: In xv6, CPU multiplexing requires leaving one kernel thread and resuming another. The supplied source describes the mechanics, the registers involved, and the scheduler's role.

1. A context switch occurs when a CPU stops executing one kernel thread and later resumes a different kernel thread.
2. The function swtch() saves the switched-from thread's CPU registers and restores the previously saved registers of the switched-to thread.
3. A thread's state consists of data in memory, such as its stack, plus its CPU registers.
4. Different threads keep their data in different areas of RAM; the CPU has only one set of registers.
5. On RISC-V, swtch saves callee-saved registers (ra, sp, s0..s11) but not caller-saved registers.
6. The RISC-V calling convention requires the compiler to generate instructions that save caller-saved registers to the stack before a function call and restore them when the function returns.
7. Each process's struct proc includes a struct context that holds the thread's saved registers when it is not running.
8. The CPU's scheduler thread's struct context is in that CPU's struct cpu.
9. A kernel thread gives up the CPU by context-switching to that CPU's scheduler thread; the scheduler thread picks a different process's kernel thread to run, and context-switches to that thread.

Question: According to the supplied source, what does a context switch preserve and restore, and what role does the scheduler thread play in xv6 CPU multiplexing?
questions.answer: A context switch preserves and restores CPU registers: swtch() saves the switched-from thread's CPU registers and restores the previously saved registers of the switched-to thread. Thread memory does not need to be saved and restored because different threads keep their data in different areas of RAM, but the CPU has only one set of registers. On RISC-V, swtch saves callee-saved registers (ra, sp, s0..s11) but not caller-saved registers, relying on the calling function to have saved caller-saved registers if needed. In xv6, a kernel thread gives up the CPU by context-switching to that CPU's scheduler thread; the scheduler thread picks a different process's kernel thread to run and context-switches to that thread.
questions.explanation: The source states the definition of a context switch and explains that swtch() saves the current CPU registers and restores the switched-to thread's saved registers. It notes that thread memory is already separated in RAM, so only the single set of CPU registers must be switched. On RISC-V, swtch handles callee-saved registers while caller-saved registers are handled by the calling function per the calling convention. The scheduler thread acts as the intermediary: a thread switches to the scheduler, and the scheduler selects and switches to another process's kernel thread.

State that the scheduler thread receives control from the yielding thread and chooses another process's kernel thread to resume.

response.answer: According to the supplied source, a context switch preserves and restores CPU registers. The swtch() function in xv6 saves the switched-from kernel thread's current CPU registers into that thread's struct context, and restores the previously saved registers from the switched-to thread's struct context into the CPU. Thread memory, such as stacks, is not saved/restored because different threads keep their data in different RAM areas, while the CPU has only one set of registers. On RISC-V, swtch saves callee-saved registers (ra, sp, s0..s11) but not caller-saved registers; the calling convention requires the caller to have already saved any caller-saved registers it needs across the call. Each process's struct proc includes a struct context for its saved registers, and each CPU's scheduler thread has its struct context in that CPU's struct cpu. In xv6 CPU multiplexing, a kernel thread gives up the CPU by context-switching to that CPU's scheduler thread; the scheduler thread then picks a different process's kernel thread to run and context-switches to that thread. xv6 thus does not directly switch from one process's kernel thread to another; the scheduler thread is the intermediary that selects and resumes the next runnable process.

Paragraph: In xv6, CPU multiplexing requires leaving one kernel thread and resuming another. The supplied source describes the mechanics, the registers involved, and the scheduler's role.

1. A context switch occurs when a CPU stops executing one kernel thread and later resumes a different kernel thread.
2. The function swtch() saves the switched-from thread's CPU registers and restores the previously saved registers of the switched-to thread.
3. A thread's state consists of data in memory, such as its stack, plus its CPU registers.
4. Different threads keep their data in different areas of RAM; the CPU has only one set of registers.
5. On RISC-V, swtch saves callee-saved registers (ra, sp, s0..s11) but not caller-saved registers.
6. The RISC-V calling convention requires the compiler to generate instructions that save caller-saved registers to the stack before a function call and restore them when the function returns.
7. Each process's struct proc includes a struct context that holds the thread's saved registers when it is not running.
8. The CPU's scheduler thread's struct context is in that CPU's struct cpu.
9. A kernel thread gives up the CPU by context-switching to that CPU's scheduler thread; the scheduler thread picks a different process's kernel thread to run, and context-switches to that thread.

Question: According to the supplied source, what does a context switch preserve and restore, and what role does the scheduler thread play in xv6 CPU multiplexing?
questions.answer: A context switch preserves and restores CPU registers: swtch() saves the switched-from thread's CPU registers and restores the previously saved registers of the switched-to thread. Thread memory does not need to be saved and restored because different threads keep their data in different areas of RAM, but the CPU has only one set of registers. On RISC-V, swtch saves callee-saved registers (ra, sp, s0..s11) but not caller-saved registers, relying on the calling function to have saved caller-saved registers if needed. In xv6, a kernel thread gives up the CPU by context-switching to that CPU's scheduler thread; the scheduler thread picks a different process's kernel thread to run and context-switches to that thread.

The scheduler thread acts as the intermediary: a thread switches to the scheduler, and the scheduler selects and switches to another process's kernel thread.

sources.text:
Any operating system is likely to run with more processes than the computer has CPUs, so a plan is needed to time-share the CPUs among the processes. Ideally the sharing would be transparent to user processes. A common approach is to provide each process with the illusion that it has its own virtual CPU by multiplexing the processes onto the hardware CPUs. This chapter explains how xv6 achieves this multiplexing.

8.1 Multiplexing

Xv6 multiplexes by switching each CPU from one process to another in two situations. First, xv6 switches when a process makes a system call that blocks (has to wait), for example read or wait. Second, xv6 periodically forces a switch to cope with processes that compute for long periods without blocking. The former are called voluntary switches, the latter involuntary.

Implementing multiplexing poses a few challenges. First, how to switch from one process to another? The basic idea is to save and restore CPU registers, though the fact that this cannot be expressed in C makes it tricky. Second, how to force switches in a way that is transparent to user processes? Xv6 uses the standard technique in which a hardware timer’s interrupts drive context switches. Third, all of the CPUs switch among the same set of processes, so a locking plan is necessary to avoid mistakes such as two CPUs deciding to run the same process at the same time. Fourth, a process’s memory and other resources must be freed when the process exits, but it cannot finish all of this itself. Fifth, each CPU of a multi-core machine must remember which process it is executing so that system calls affect the correct process’s kernel state.

8.2 Context switch overview

The term “context switch” refers to the steps involved in a CPU leaving off execution of one kernel thread (usually for later resumption), and resuming execution of a different kernel thread; this switching is the heart of multiplexing. Xv6 does not directly context switch from one process’s kernel thread to another process’s kernel thread; instead, a kernel thread gives up the CPU by context-switching to that CPU’s “scheduler thread,” and the scheduler thread picks a different process’s kernel thread to run, and context-switches to that thread.

At a broader scope, the steps involved in switching from one user process to another are illustrated in Figure 8.1: a trap (system call or interrupt) from the old process’s user space to its kernel thread, a context switch to the current CPU’s scheduler thread, a context switch to a new process’s kernel thread, and a trap return to the user-level process.

8.3 Code: Context switching

The function swtch() in kernel/swtch.S contains the heart of thread context switching: it saves the switched-from thread’s CPU registers, and restores the previously-saved registers of the switched-to thread. The basic reason this is sufficient is that a thread’s state consist of data in memory (e.g. its stack) plus its CPU registers; thread memory need not saved and restored because different threads keep their data in different areas of RAM; but the CPU has only one set of registers so they must be switched (saved and restored) between threads.

Each thread’s struct proc includes a struct context that holds the thread’s saved registers when it is not running. A CPU’s scheduler thread’s struct context is in that CPU’s struct cpu. When thread X wishes to switch to thread Y, thread X calls swtch(&X’s context, &Y’s context). swtch() saves the current CPU registers in X’s context, then loads the content of Y’s context into the CPU registers, then returns.

swtch saves callee-saved registers (ra,sp,s0..s11) but not caller-saved registers. The RISC-V calling convention requires that if code needs to preserve the value in a caller-saved register across a function call, the compiler must generate instructions that save the register to the stack before the function call, and restore from the stack when the function returns. So swtch can rely on the function that called it having already saved the caller-saved registers (either that, or the calling function didn’t need the values in the registers).
